summary: This document defines a new IKEv2 Traffic Selector type, TS_SECLABEL, so peers can negotiate Mandatory Access Control security labels as part of the Security Policy Database. This is called Labeled IPsec. The label is carried as a variable-length opaque field.

plainLanguage.summary: Some secure places put colored badges on everything, and only matching badges may mix. This lets two computers agree on those badges when they set up a private tunnel.

questions: how do ikev2 security labels work
subtitle: A new IKEv2 Traffic Selector type that lets two IPsec peers agree on a Mandatory Access Control security label for a tunnel.

tldr.problem: IPsec Traffic Selectors could only match on IP addresses, protocol and ports, so peers had no way to negotiate Mandatory Access Control security labels such as SELinux contexts.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds the TS Type TS_SECLABEL, value 10, carrying an opaque security label that must accompany an IP address selector and is matched exactly.
tldr.outcome: Peers can restrict a Child SA to traffic with a negotiated label, known as Labeled IPsec.

today: RFC 9478 is a Proposed Standard, published in October 2023, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Security Labels and IPsec
sections.content:
In Mandatory Access Control (MAC) systems, every subject and object has a security label made of security attributes, and a system policy decides access from them. Older Multi-Level Secure systems used a sensitivity level and a compartment (RFC 5570). SELinux uses colon-separated ASCII strings of identity, role and type, often called security contexts.

In IPsec, Traffic Selector (TS) payloads say which packets may flow over a new Security Association, as enforced by the Security Policy Database (SPD, RFC 4301). This RFC adds a TS Type, TS_SECLABEL, to IKEv2 so labels can be negotiated as extra selectors that narrow what traffic the SA may carry.
sections.plainLanguage: A tunnel normally only checks the address on a package. Now it can also check the colored badge on the package.

sections.title: Traffic Selector Terms
sections.content:
RFC 7296 uses the term Traffic Selector both for a TS payload and for the individual selectors in it. The RFC clarifies the terms. A Traffic Selector is one selector of a specific TS Type. A TS payload is a set of one or more Traffic Selectors of the same or different types.

The example given is a TS_IPV4_ADDR_RANGE selector for UDP (protocol 17) in 198.51.100.0/24 covering all ports, written (17, 0, 198.51.100.0-198.51.100.255). Alone in a payload it is written TS((17, 0, 198.51.100.0-198.51.100.255)).
sections.plainLanguage: One selector is a single rule. A payload is the whole list of rules handed over together.

sections.title: The TS_SECLABEL Payload
sections.content:
The selector has a one-octet TS Type set to 10, a one-octet Reserved field, a two-octet Selector Length (the length of the substructure including the header), and a Security Label, an opaque byte stream of at least one octet.

The label is opaque to IKE: the implementation may know nothing about its meaning beyond treating it as a type and a value to pass to the SPD. It is assumed the IKE implementation can match the label against its own configured value.
sections.plainLanguage: The badge is a sealed label. The tunnel software does not need to read it, only compare it with the one it expects.

sections.title: Rules for TS_SECLABEL
sections.content:
TS_SECLABEL does not support narrowing or wildcards; it MUST be an exact match. It MUST NOT be the only TS Type in a TS payload, and an IP address selector such as TS_IPV4_ADDR_RANGE or TS_IPV6_ADDR_RANGE MUST accompany it. If a payload arrives with only TS_SECLABEL types, the exchange MUST be aborted with an Error Notify message containing TS_UNACCEPTABLE.

A zero-length label MUST NOT be used. A payload with a zero-length label MUST be ignored, and if no other payload has an acceptable label the exchange MUST be aborted with TS_UNACCEPTABLE. A zero-length label MUST NOT be read as a wildcard.

If several labels are allowed for an address range, protocol and port range, the initiator includes all of them and the responder MUST select exactly one. The responder MUST then use that label for all selector operations on the resulting TS, even if it considers the label optional.
sections.plainLanguage: The badge must match exactly, a blank badge is not allowed, and if you offer several badges the other side picks exactly one.

sections.title: Negotiating the Selector
sections.content:
When the initiator's TSi contains a TS_SECLABEL along with another type, the responder builds its answer for the other types using their normal rules (such as narrowing), then adds exactly one TS_SECLABEL. If it cannot, it MUST return a TS_UNACCEPTABLE Error Notify payload.

If the label is optional in the initiator's configuration and the responder's reply includes a TS_SECLABEL, the Child SA MUST be created with that label. If the reply lacks one, the initiator installs the Child SA without a label. If the initiator required the label, it MUST NOT install the Child SA and MUST send a Delete notification so the responder can remove its side.

The RFC's example has the initiator offering several address ranges plus two labels, TS_SECLABEL1 and TS_SECLABEL2, in both TSi and TSr, and the responder answering with one narrowed range and TS_SECLABEL1 in each.

TSi and TSr could carry different labels, though the RFC calls that unlikely. An initiator that does not want this should first try a Child SA with only the first label and, on failure, retry with only the second. If different IP ranges may only use different specific labels, they should be negotiated in separate Child SA negotiations and MUST NOT be combined.
sections.plainLanguage: You offer a list of badges, the other side picks one, and if badges were required and it picks none, you tear the tunnel down.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
A packet that matches an SPD entry in every component except the label is treated as not matching. If no other SPD entry matches, that mislabeled traffic might be sent in the clear. The RFC presumes other MAC methods keep mislabeled traffic from reaching IPsec, or that the IPsec subsystem installs a REJECT/DISCARD rule so unlabeled traffic matching a labeled rule is not sent unprotected.

IANA added value 10, TS_SECLABEL, to the IKEv2 Traffic Selector Types registry, with this RFC as the reference.
sections.plainLanguage: If a package has the wrong badge, it must be stopped, not waved through without protection.
